title: August 2026 close, distribution and service
notice: Every figure, name and sentence in this file is invented for training. Halyard Provisioning Group does not exist. Nothing here is drawn from any real company, engagement or dataset.

company.name: Halyard Provisioning Group, Inc.
company.profile: Food service distribution and equipment maintenance, four regional depots, roughly $85 million of annual revenue and 240 employees. Privately held, revolver in place, monthly close on the fifth business day.

materiality.basis: Accounts shown are those with activity in either month.

margin_definition: Product gross margin is account 4000 less account 5000, divided by account 4000. Supplier rebates in account 4300 are recorded as other income and are outside the margin calculation.

subtotals.label: Total revenue
subtotals.note: Supplier rebates in account 4300 are other income and are not in this total.

subtotals.label: Operating expense
subtotals.note: Every account from 6000 down. Cost of product sold and inbound freight are outside it.

commentary.author: Assistant controller, drafted with the close assistant and lightly edited

sentences.text: Product gross margin held at 22 percent in both July and August once rounded, so the channel mix did not move.
Distribution revenue of $5,905,000 rose 9.4 percent on share gains in the independent restaurant channel.
Service revenue grew $111,000 on maintenance contract renewals in the Southline territory.
Three August freight invoices totaling $31,200 were posted to September because the vendor portal closed early.
Temporary labor rose $86,800 to cover the summer peak at the Northgate depot.

Bad debt expense rose $1,700 because one Southline account moved past ninety days, the reserve percentage for that aging bucket is unchanged at 15 percent, and the customer has since agreed a payment plan that we expect to hold.
Insurance was flat at $47,300 because the policy amortises straight line to March 2027 and no endorsement was issued in the month.
Warehouse wages fell 4.8 percent on the productivity program launched at the start of the month.
Marketing fell $67,500 as the trade show accrual carried in July was released into August expense ahead of the September show.
No new legal matters arose during August.
The legal settlement accrual of $185,000 covers the delivery claim notified to the broker in August and will be reversed once the release is signed.
Inventory shrink fell $44,800 because of the same warehouse productivity program that reduced warehouse wages.

counterparty.note: That account is the denominator in the margin definition given above the table.

answer_key.claim: The memo says product gross margin held at 22 percent in both months once rounded, so channel mix did not move.
answer_key.correct: July margin was 23.5 percent, being $1,267,000 on $5,398,000. August margin was 21.9 percent, being $1,293,000 on $5,905,000. July does not round to 22 percent at all, and the real movement is a decline of 1.6 points worth roughly $93,000 of margin at August revenue. The conclusion that mix did not move is contradicted by the numbers used to reach it.

focus.what: August freight invoices the memo posts to September

answer_key.claim: The memo says August invoices were posted to September because the vendor portal closed early.
answer_key.correct: August freight is an August cost. A vendor portal date does not change the period a cost belongs to. The account moved $27,600 in the month and the deferred amount is $31,200, which is larger than the movement recorded, so August freight is understated by more than it appears to have risen unless an accrual was posted. The memo offers a system reason in place of an accounting answer.

answer_key.claim: The memo gives bad debt expense the longest explanation in the document.
answer_key.correct: The movement is $1,700 and 17.9 percent, which clears the percentage leg and fails the dollar leg, so no commentary is due. It takes three clauses while a $172,000 rebate movement takes none, and the payment plan expectation adds a forward looking claim to a line that did not need commentary at all.

counterparty.note: Both movements are at the same depot in the same month, and the memo explains only one of them.

answer_key.claim: The memo presents the fall in warehouse wages as a productivity program.
answer_key.correct: Warehouse wages fell $37,700 while temporary labor rose $86,800 at the same depot in the same month. Total labor cost rose $49,100. A cost that moved between two accounts is presented as a saving, and the memo explains only the half that looks good.

answer_key.claim: The memo attributes revenue growth to share gains in the independent restaurant channel.
answer_key.correct: Share gain is a market claim and nothing in the schedule supports it. There is no channel split, no customer count, no case volume and no market data. Growth of $507,000 in one month has no evidenced driver.

answer_key.claim: The memo says service revenue grew $111,000.
answer_key.correct: Service revenue fell $111,000, from $1,096,000 to $985,000, a decline of 10.1 percent. The memo states a decline as growth, and the renewal story then explains a movement that did not happen.

answer_key.claim: The memo never mentions supplier rebates.
answer_key.correct: Supplier rebates rose $172,000, from $42,000 to $214,000, an increase of 410 percent. It is one of the largest movements in the month, it lands in other income, and it carries no commentary. A rebate spike of that size usually means a volume tier was reached or a prior period true-up was booked, and both change how the month should be read.

counterparty.note: The memo offers that account's movement as the reason this one moved.

answer_key.claim: The memo explains the fall in inventory shrink by the warehouse productivity program that reduced warehouse wages.
answer_key.correct: A wage saving does not produce a shrink reduction. The two accounts measure different things: shrink is a count or costing variance and wages are a payroll cost. Warehouse wages fell only because the labour moved to temporary labor in account 6050, so the driver the memo borrows did not happen either. The $44,800 shrink reversal is unexplained, and a swing of that size after a $62,300 rise in the prior month is the first thing to ask about.

answer_key.claim: The memo says the July trade show accrual was released into August expense ahead of the September show.
answer_key.correct: A cost for a September event belongs in September, not in July and not in August. The July treatment was wrong and moving it to August does not fix it: the amount should sit in prepaid expense until the show takes place. The memo describes a second wrong period as though it were a correction.

answer_key.claim: One sentence says no new legal matters arose in August and the next books a $185,000 accrual for a claim notified in August.
answer_key.correct: S10 and S11 cannot sit in the same memo. A delivery claim notified to the broker in August is a new legal matter in August, so either S10 is false or the notification date in S11 is wrong. A reader signing this memo is signing both statements.

distractors.text: Depot repairs rose 23 percent and the memo does not mention them anywhere. Obtain the contractor schedule and the open purchase orders before this memo is released.
distractors.why_wrong: The movement is $8,400 against a $25,000 threshold. It clears the percentage leg and fails the dollar leg, and the rule requires both, so no commentary is due. The reviewer should reject this challenge.

distractors.text: Fleet fuel of $129,400 in August is well above the $91,200 it carried in June, so the invoice cutoff problem has repeated for a third month. Obtain the fuel card report for June, July and August.
distractors.why_wrong: This schedule compares August to July, and July carried $122,800. June is not on this pack at all. Against the prior column the movement is $6,600, which fails both legs of the threshold, and the challenge builds its conclusion on a month the reader cannot see. The reviewer should reject this challenge.

distractors.text: Insurance shows no movement at all across the two months. Ask the controller to confirm that the policy is being amortised and that no endorsement was issued, because a nil variance can hide a missed accrual.
distractors.why_wrong: S7 states both facts, and a nil variance is exactly what a straight line policy amortisation looks like. The challenge asks back what the memo has already answered, on a movement of zero that fails both legs of the threshold. The reviewer should reject this challenge.
